newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: IVORIAN COCOA EXPORTERS SAY COULD MANAGE AUCTION.
newsitem.headline: IVORIAN COCOA EXPORTERS SAY COULD MANAGE AUCTION.

text.p: Ivorian cocoa exporters could manage their own cocoa auction and ensure forward sales if donors succeed in reducing the state's role, exporters said on Wednesday.
"If GEPEX (exporters' trade body) was approached I do not think it would have a problem," said one GEPEX member.
Ivory Coast has loosened its monopoly on cocoa and coffee marketing since 1995 under terms of a $150 million agriculture credit from the World Bank -- which wants further changes.
Cocoa and coffee liberalisation are on the agenda for donor talks next week on a three-year economic plan for Ivory Coast and an IMF Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility.
Donors want the state commodities board Caistab to hand farm-to-port price-setting to the private sector, with exporters possibly assuming a greater role in export auction management.
Ivory Coast has agreed to sweeping coffee marketing reforms from 1998/99, and from 1999/2000 for cocoa, but full details have yet to be decided and officially announced.
But it still sets annual farm-to-port marketing prices, called a bareme, which donors want ended to help raise the level of FOB prices paid to farmers -- now one of the world's lowest at 40 percent.

The Caistab has since May 1996 managed a cocoa and coffee auction, replacing telephone deals, to raise market transparency and efficiency. Donors say price liberalisation will cut the need for selling forward two-thirds of each year's cocoa export contracts before marketing seasons open.
Exporters want auction sales spread over 12 months.
Ending cocoa auctions would mean cocoa arriving at ports in one go during the harvesting peak between October and January, filling warehouses to capacity, they say.
"Port storage would have to be doubled along with more ships. It would be a difficult market to manage," one said.
"If private operators are unable to guarantee export contracts that would affect everyone, particularly industry," said one exporter. "We need an impartial marketing body."
Exporters point to Brazil's price liberalisation while keeping forward sales.
"The Caistab might no longer be responsible, but there is no reason why private operators should not step in."
One Ivorian buyer of cocoa, Omais, is building a large cocoa warehouse in the second port of San Pedro. Other forwarders and exporters are also building up capacity.
"People are preparing. If everyone sees warehouses are full, (world) prices could fall until they are emptier," said one exporter, citing Ivory Coast's 40 percent share of world production.
"A million plus tonnes would have to be sold on a spot basis," and some cocoa would be stored upcountry with a consequent quality risk, he added.

Ivorian cocoa warehouses filled to an estimated capacity of 400,000 tonnes in early 1996. Some exporters put that down to breaches of auction rules as contracts were held back as world prices rose. Limited auction reforms have been agreed for 1997/98 (Oct-Sept) after complaints of overbidding and concentration of contracts in a few hands. --Abidjan newsroom, + 225 21 90 90
